claimBlocks.suggestedSection: Homelands across a later international border
claimBlocks.text: The Ktunaxa Nation Council describes homelands along the Kootenay and Columbia rivers and Arrow Lakes, extending historically beyond British Columbia into neighboring provinces and U.S. states, including Idaho. Its accompanying map expressly warns that its boundaries are not comprehensive or exhaustive. This community account connects land, seasonal livelihoods and stewardship without defining a single modern government or final legal boundary.

claimBlocks.suggestedSection: Language work and distinct participating communities
claimBlocks.text: The Council's public language article describes work with speakers from four Canadian First Nations, the Kootenai Tribe of Idaho and Montana's Ksanka Band of the Confederated Salish and Kootenai Tribes. It connects classes, curriculum and community activities with intergenerational relationships. This is an institutional account of language work, without a verified speaker census or proof that every participating community operates identical programs.
claimBlocks.sourceLocator: Colonial disruption and community-specific program discussion, lines 94–114, especially 102–112

claimBlocks.suggestedSection: An Idaho community's history of remaining and organizing
claimBlocks.text: The Kootenai Tribe of Idaho describes a separately governed community within the broader Ktunaxa world. Its history recounts pressure to relocate to Montana, remaining near Bonners Ferry, and peaceful protest in 1974 against neglect and inadequate living conditions. This is the Idaho Tribe's own account of dispossession and self-determination, not a single political history for all Ktunaxa communities.
claimBlocks.sourceLocator: Actual Tribal History body 55–85; contemporary institutional self-description 85–88

claimBlocks.text: The Tribe-hosted Constitution and Bylaws records adoption on April 10, 1947, followed by federal approval on June 16. The compilation labels its latest amendment 1996. Its framework assigns a Tribal Council powers to represent the Tribe, manage affairs and establish a court and law code. This is a dated institutional text, without independently verifying all current amendments or rules.
claimBlocks.sourceLocator: PDF 1 compilation header and Article III; 2 Article IV; 4 adoption certificate; 5 federal approval

claimBlocks.suggestedSection: River restoration as a Tribal priority
claimBlocks.text: The Idaho Tribe's restoration materials connect changes to the Kootenai River—dikes, agriculture, logging, mining and dams—with diminished habitat and subsistence access. Its aquaculture account places fish conservation within an ecosystem approach involving Tribal, First Nations and government partners. These are program descriptions and goals, without independently establishing current population recovery or every claimed legal right.
claimBlocks.sourceLocator: Habitat Restoration 55–65; Aquaculture 49–62; overlapping Fish & Wildlife 52–57

claimBlocks.suggestedSection: Canadian Council work and community-driven planning
claimBlocks.text: The Council's 2026 annual report describes education outreach, tutoring, training support and youth engagement in its Canadian member communities. Its governance chapter discusses data sovereignty and community-driven decision making. These are dated institutional reports and proposals, distinct from the Idaho Tribe's government. The report's draft governance goals do not establish completed agreements or verified outcomes.
claimBlocks.sourceLocator: Actual report 2, 4, 38–41, 53–55; 55 explicitly marks governance goal Draft

claimBlocks.text: The Idaho Tribe's short education page describes school support, adult learning and assistance for higher education. It is a useful access point; the undated description does not establish current eligibility, availability or outcomes.

initialAdequacy.rationale: Six substantive selected works/collections support a considerably stronger Idaho-centered introduction, with cross-border context. The final integrated profile and its broader Ktunaxa representation have not been independently assessed; source quantity alone does not assign adequacy.
remainingLimits: Independent Montana-community perspectives are limited to explicit peer identification in these sources.
The Canadian Council's work is not a substitute for the four member First Nations' own detailed histories.
Current law, program outcomes and quantitative language conditions remain outside the review.

researchGaps: Further Idaho-community oral-history/public interview perspectives, and original historical records, would broaden the institutional accounts without substituting a colonial author's voice for the Tribe's own.
Separate substantive Ksanka/Kootenai community sources in Montana remain a priority; Salish and Upper Pend d'Oreille people are not interchangeable with Kootenai people within CSKT.
The Canadian Council report and map are situated institutional perspectives, not exhaustive research into each member Nation, boundary, title claim or land declaration.
An actual specialist language-learning publication and dated evaluation would strengthen the public program descriptions. No current speaker census or tested fluency outcome was established.
Restoration technical plans and monitoring studies remain unread; no claim that plans, hatchery work or institutional goals establish completed ecological recovery.
